t: Minimum Cost of a Path With Special Roads — Dijkstra on Endpoints
o: Travel cost between points is Manhattan distance; special roads give one-directional discounted edges (usable repeatedly). Only points that appear as special-road endpoints (plus start and target) can ever be worth standing on — at most 402 nodes. Build a complete graph over these nodes weighted by Manhattan distance, add special edges with their costs, and run Dijkstra from start. Example 2 shows sometimes the direct Manhattan path is optimal.
k: Intermediate positions other than special endpoints/start/target are never beneficial — Manhattan travel between graph nodes covers everything else.
Graph has ≤ 2m + 2 nodes and O(m²) edges; Dijkstra handles it easily.

a.i: Node list = start, target, and both endpoints of each special road. Edges: pairwise Manhattan weights, plus directed special edges (a→b, cost). Run Dijkstra from start; answer is dist[target].
s: Build adjacency: for all pairs (i,j) weight Manhattan(p_i, p_j); for each special road add directed edge with its cost if cheaper than walking.
Dijkstra from start's index; return dist[target's index].
a.t: O(m² log m) — dense graph over ≤ 2m+2 nodes with Dijkstra using a heap.

a.i: Since any optimal route uses at most m special roads, relaxing 'walk anywhere + take any special road' repeatedly m+1 times converges. Keep dist[] over the same node set; each round updates every node from every node via Manhattan distance and applies special edges. O(m³) ≈ 8·10^6 — simple and heap-free.
s: Repeat m+1 times: for each ordered pair (u,v) relax dist[v] via dist[u] + Manhattan; for each special road relax its head via its tail + cost.
a.t: O(m³) — m+1 rounds of all-pairs relaxation over ≤ 2m+2 nodes; fine for m ≤ 200.
a.sp: O(m²) implicit via point list; O(m) for dist arrays.

w: Dijkstra is the standard answer; the relaxation version is a neat fallback when you forget heap details. Pitfalls: special roads are directed (example 2 exploits this), duplicate endpoints (dedupe or just overwrite — taking min keeps correctness), and remembering you can always walk directly between any two graph nodes. Follow-up: bidirectional special roads, or limited number of road uses (then layered Dijkstra).
